title: Six Simple Ways to Add More Protein to Your Child's Diet
excerpt: Eggs, nut butters, Greek yogurt, stuffed parathas, sprouted moong and smoothies — six breakfast-friendly ways to raise a child's protein without a mealtime fight, plus how much children actually need.
body:
• Protein builds muscle, supports brain development and keeps children's energy levels stable through the day, according to The Times of India — but getting enough into picky eaters is the hard part.
  • Six breakfast-friendly fixes: eggs in any form, nut butters on toast or fruit, Greek yogurt bowls, protein-stuffed parathas, sprouted moong dishes, and milk-based smoothies.
  • How much is enough: Nestle's expert guide, citing WHO figures for Indian children, puts the need at about 1.2 grams of protein per kg of body weight a day for ages 1-3, about 1 gram for ages 4-6, and about 0.9 grams for ages 7-9.
  • One egg provides about 7 grams of protein and a cup of milk about 8 grams — spacing roughly five protein portions across the day can meet a young child's requirement.

Every parent knows the standoff: the nutrient matters, the child is not interested. Protein helps build muscles, supports brain development and keeps energy levels stable throughout the day, The Times of India notes — the challenge is sneaking more of it into meals a child will actually eat. These six approaches, drawn from the Times of India's guide and Nestle's expert advice, work with breakfasts and snacks Indian families already make.

1. Start With Eggs

Eggs are the simplest lever. Serve them boiled, scrambled, as omelettes, or as mini egg muffins with vegetables and cheese; for picky eaters, the Times of India suggests cutting hard-boiled eggs into shapes or turning an omelette into a roll or sandwich. Nestle's guide adds masala fried or poached eggs with toast or roti for children bored with boiled eggs, and notes an egg contains around 7 grams of protein.

2. Swap Butter for Nut Butters

Replace regular butter with peanut, almond or cashew butter, which carry protein and healthy fats. Spread them on whole-grain toast, chapati rolls, or fruit slices such as apple or banana. The Times of India advises choosing unsweetened nut butter, smooth for younger children; Nestle's guide adds a necessary caution — make sure your child is not allergic to peanuts.

3. Use Greek Yogurt

Greek yogurt contains twice the protein of regular curd, according to the Times of India, with a thick, creamy texture children tend to accept. Mix it with fruit, a little honey, or homemade granola for a breakfast bowl. Yoghurt also brings gut-friendly bacteria that aid digestion, Nestle notes, and works beyond breakfast in raitas and smoothies.

4. Stuff the Paratha

Parathas are already a child favorite; the upgrade is the filling. Stuff them with paneer, moong dal, boiled egg or soya keema, and pair with a little curd or a glass of milk for a high-protein, desi-style breakfast. Nestle's guide makes the same point with paneer paratha and adds idli with lentil sambar and soy upma as carb-based meals that quietly carry protein.

5. Sprout Moong

Sprouted moong beans are a light, plant-based protein source that can become moong chillas, pancakes or kebabs, or be folded into upma or poha. Sprouts are easy to digest, the Times of India notes, which makes them a practical daily option rather than an occasional health food.

6. Blend It Into a Smoothie

For children who resist milk on its own, Nestle's expert guide to adding protein to a child's diet suggests smoothies built on milk with nut butter, yoghurt or chia seeds, sweetened with fresh fruit. The same guide suggests protein snacks — yoghurt, string cheese, baked chicken, fish fingers — for children who miss protein at mealtimes.

How Much Protein Is Actually Enough?

The targets are smaller than the marketing suggests. Citing WHO figures for Indian children, Nestle puts the recommended intake at about 1.2 grams per kilogram of body weight per day for ages 1 to 3, about 1 gram for ages 4 to 6, and about 0.9 grams for ages 7 to 9. With an egg at roughly 7 grams and a cup (244 grams) of milk at 8 grams, spacing about five protein portions across the day can meet a young child's requirement. The risk of deficiency is higher for children on vegetarian diets, which cut out egg, meat, fish and poultry — for those families, the dal, paneer, sprouts, nut butters and yogurt above do the heavy lifting.
